title: Over 160,000 Flee South Africa as Anti-Immigrant Violence Tears Through Economy
excerpt: A mass exodus of migrant workers is disrupting delivery services, domestic work, and textile manufacturing as vigilante groups escalate door-to-door campaigns across the country.
body:
• More than 160,000 migrants have fled South Africa since late May, with Zimbabwe alone reporting nearly 100,000 returnees and Nigeria evacuating 1,490 citizens on chartered flights.
  • The departure of foreign workers is disrupting key sectors: e-hailing services report driver shortages, domestic worker bookings have crashed to pandemic-era levels, and a major textile hub has lost 15% of its workforce.
  • The "March and March" movement has shifted to weekly Thursday door-to-door campaigns targeting immigrants after its June 30 deadline passed, with vigilantes demanding documentation and forcing shop closures.
  • President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed to crack down on groups inciting violence, while the economic fallout threatens to deepen South Africa's unemployment crisis rather than ease it.

South Africa's worst wave of xenophobic violence in nearly two decades has triggered a mass exodus of migrant workers, draining labor from critical sectors of Africa's largest economy and drawing international condemnation.

Authorities have processed around 67,000 migrants for deportation or voluntary repatriation in recent weeks, according to Bloomberg, but the true scale is far larger. Zimbabwe alone says nearly 100,000 citizens have returned since late May. Nigeria completed the evacuation of 1,490 nationals on five chartered flights, with the latest arriving in Lagos on July 15, according to Reuters.

Door-to-Door Hunts in Soweto

The crisis is being driven by the "March and March" movement, led by former radio presenter Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, which has organized protests across major cities since April. After setting a June 30 deadline for all undocumented migrants to leave, the movement shifted to weekly door-to-door campaigns every Thursday.

https://x.com/UKWELINEWSWORLD/status/2079461120264282497

In Soweto, mobs armed with sticks and baseball bats have gone street by street, demanding police "arrest all foreigners on sight" and handing out pamphlets designed to look like eviction notices, according to Sky News reporting from inside the campaigns. Citizen arrests for immigration offenses — illegal under South African law — continue at pace.

"When all of them are gone. Not 80 per cent gone, when all of them are gone. Then I will say my job is done."

— John Nhlanhla Mncube, Freedom Park March and March leader

Ngobese-Zuma has declared that Ubuntu, the African humanist principle of togetherness celebrated in South African culture, is "suspended until further notice." More than 50,000 immigrants — mostly from Malawi, Zimbabwe, and Mozambique — have been repatriated or deported since the June 30 deadline.

An Economy Losing Its Workers

The departures are sending tremors through sectors that depend heavily on migrant labor. SweepSouth, an app connecting domestic workers with households, recorded its highest rate of lost bookings since the Covid pandemic during the week of June 30. On that day alone, cancellations surpassed a typical month's total, CEO Lourandi Kriel told Bloomberg.

At least half of e-hailing drivers are migrant workers, according to the National E-Hailing Federation of South Africa, and a noticeable absence of drivers has pushed up trip prices since the protests peaked. Migrants account for 70% of Shoprite Holdings' Sixty60 delivery fleet of nearly 10,000 motorcycle riders. One Johannesburg-based driver from Lesotho told Bloomberg that seven of the 10 riders he started with in June have already left the country.

In Newcastle, a key textile hub in KwaZulu-Natal, hundreds of foreign workers have gone home. The Southern African Clothing and Textile Workers' Union estimates 15% of the workforce has fled, with little prospect of replacement — local workers demand higher wages that barely cover commuting costs.

"A fast outflow of migrant workers could hamper productivity and production in the near term and may slow economic growth."

— Mpho Lenoke, North-West University economics programme leader

International Backlash Mounts

The violence has drawn sharp international response. Ghana has petitioned the African Union over South Africa's treatment of Ghanaians and is compiling a list of assets lost by its nationals for potential litigation. Nigeria condemned the deaths of at least two nationals allegedly assaulted by South African security officials. Mozambique has reported five citizens killed in attacks.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the violence a "tragic betrayal" of the African nations that supported South Africa during the struggle against apartheid. South Africa's justice minister Mmamoloko Kubayi warned that the backlash is damaging the country's global image, with South African artists seeing gigs cancelled across the continent.

Human Rights Watch has documented vigilantes targeting both African and Asian foreign nationals, noting that attacks occur in broad daylight with insufficient police response. The rights group called on authorities to bring perpetrators to justice rather than allow the violence to continue.

Roots of the Crisis

South Africa's unemployment rate stands at nearly 33%, the highest in the world. Migration to the country has actually decreased over the past decade — from 615,000 arrivals in 2015 to about 150,000 in 2025, according to the World Bank — but anti-immigrant sentiment has intensified ahead of November's local elections, with politicians pledging immigration crackdowns to win votes.

A central bank-backed report estimates South Africa's migrant population at 3.9 million, of which 89% are undocumented. Nearly half are from Zimbabwe, with Malawi and Mozambique each accounting for over 630,000. Remittances from South Africa to labor-sending nations reached a record R19.4 billion ($1.2 billion) in 2024 — flows now at risk.

What to Watch

President Ramaphosa has pledged to set up dedicated immigration courts, replace paper identity documents with biometric digital ID cards, and work with neighboring countries on root causes. But whether these measures can contain the vigilante movement while addressing legitimate public frustration over unemployment and crime remains an open question. The Indian community in South Africa — one of the largest outside India, concentrated in Durban and the broader KwaZulu-Natal province — is watching the unrest closely, particularly as the violence has targeted Asian foreign nationals alongside African migrants.
